How to generate a RESTful API request on Cisco Nexus Dashboard?
Version: 6.3.1
API name: get information of device connector versions

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve Device Connector Versions information from a specified URL. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. The URL points to a JSON file containing Device Connector Versions information.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the GET request as key-value pairs.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step guide on how to **generate and execute** the “Get information of device connector versions” REST API call from the Cisco Nexus Dashboard (v6.3.1). The instructions cover both the **web UI (API Explorer)** and a **command‑line / Postman** approach so you can pick the method that best fits your workflow. --- ## 1. Prerequisites | Item | What you need | How to get it | |------|---------------|---------------| | **Dashboard URL** | `https://` | From your network admin or the URL you use to log in. | | **Credentials** | Username & password (or OAuth client ID/secret) | Provided by your Nexus Dashboard administrator. | | **API Token** | Bearer token for authentication | Obtained via the `/api/v1/auth/token` endpoint (see below). | | **Device ID / Connector ID** | Optional query parameters | You can find these in the UI or via the “List devices” API. | > **Tip:** If you’re not sure what the exact query parameters are, open the API Explorer – it will show the required and optional fields. --- ## 2. Using the Cisco Nexus Dashboard UI (API Explorer) 1. **Log in** to the Nexus Dashboard web console. 2. In the left‑hand navigation pane, click **Developer Tools → API Explorer**. 3. In the search box, type **“device connector versions”** or the exact API name (`getDeviceConnectorVersions`). 4. Click the API entry to open its details page. 5. The page will display: * **Endpoint** – e.g. `GET /api/v1/device-connector-versions` * **Parameters** – query string, path, header, body (if any) * **Authentication** – usually `Bearer Token` in the `Authorization` header 6. **Fill in the parameters**: * `deviceId` – optional, filter by device * `connectorId` – optional, filter by connector * `page`, `size`, `sort` – optional pagination 7. Click the **“Generate Request”** button. * The UI will show the fully‑formed HTTP request (method, URL, headers, body). * You can copy the request text or click **“Send”** to execute it directly from the UI. 8. **View the response** – the UI will display the JSON payload, status code, and headers. > **Example** (generated request): > ``` > GET https:///api/v1/device-connector-versions?deviceId=12345 > Authorization: Bearer > Accept: application/json > ``` --- ## 3. Using cURL (Command Line) 1. **Obtain an access token** (if you don’t already have one): ```bash curl -X POST "https:///api/v1/auth/token" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"username":"","password":""}' ``` The response will contain a JSON object like: ```json {"access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."} ``` 2. **Make the API call**: ```bash curl -X GET "https:///api/v1/device-connector-versions?deviceId=12345" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." \ -H "Accept: application/json" ``` Replace the token and query parameters as needed. 3. **Inspect the output** – you’ll see a JSON array of connector versions, e.g.: ```json [ { "connectorId": "conn-001", "version": "v1.2.3", "status": "active", "releaseDate": "2024-01-15" }, ... ] ``` --- ## 4. Using Postman (Optional) 1. **Import the OpenAPI spec** (if available) from the Nexus Dashboard: * In the API Explorer, click **“Export OpenAPI Spec”** (or copy the URL to the spec). * In Postman, choose **Import → Link** and paste the spec URL. 2. Postman will create a collection with the `getDeviceConnectorVersions` request pre‑configured. 3. Set the **environment variables** (`{{baseUrl}}`, `{{token}}`) or replace them manually. 4. Hit **Send** to execute and view the response. --- ## 5. Common Pitfalls & Troubleshooting | Issue | Likely Cause | Fix | |-------|--------------|-----| | **401 Unauthorized** | Token expired or missing | Refresh token or re‑authenticate | | **404 Not Found** | Wrong endpoint or missing query param | Verify the exact path (`/api/v1/device-connector-versions`) | | **400 Bad Request** | Invalid query parameter value | Check the API docs for allowed values | | **Rate limiting** | Too many requests in a short period | Add `Retry-After` header or slow down requests | --- ## 6. Quick Reference – API Call Summary | Element | Example | |---------|---------| | **Method** | GET | | **Endpoint** | `/api/v1/device-connector-versions` | | **Base URL** | `https://` | | **Headers** | `Authorization: Bearer `
`Accept: application/json` | | **Query Params** | `deviceId`, `connectorId`, `page`, `size`, `sort` (all optional) | | **Response** | JSON array of connector version objects | --- ### Final Note The **API Explorer** is the quickest way to generate a request because it auto‑populates the URL, headers, and query parameters based on the API definition. Once you’re comfortable, you can copy the generated request into your favorite tool (curl, Postman, or your own script) and automate it as needed. Happy querying!
